This modest starting mass is characteristic of passerines that undergo a rapid growth trajectory within the sheltered environment of the woven nest. The mass gain during the first week is particularly steep, with feather tracts becoming visible as the pin feathers emerge beneath the downy coat, marking the transition from a naked neonate to a brooded nestling capable of limited thermoregulation.

This post-fledging care is crucial for survival, as the young bird must learn to identify suitable food items and avoid predators in a complex environment. The transition to nutritional independence is gradual, with the frequency of parental provisioning slowly decreasing over time as the juvenile becomes more proficient at capturing insects and other prey.

Females inspect multiple nests before selecting a mate, and the quality of the nest architecture can be a decisive factor in female choice. After pairing, the female lines the interior with soft materials and begins the incubation process, a stage during which the male may continue to build additional nests to attract other females, as this species is polygonous.
